questiontext.text: Specification mutation testing applies mutation operators to:

answer.text: A specification or model of the system (e.g. a requirement, an FSM, or a temporal-logic property), not the program source code

feedback.text: Correct — in specification mutation the artifact that is altered is the spec/model, not the code.

answer.text: The program's source code

feedback.text: Mutating source code is program (code) mutation, a different technique.

answer.text: The compiled binary of the program

feedback.text: Specification mutation works on the specification, not on compiled code.

answer.text: The test cases themselves

feedback.text: Test cases are what we evaluate or generate; specification mutation changes the spec.

generalfeedback.text: Specification mutation applies mutation operators to a specification or model — a boolean/logic requirement, a finite-state machine, or a temporal-logic property — rather than to the program's code.

questiontext.text: A mutant specification is:

answer.text: A copy of the original specification with one small change introduced by a mutation operator

feedback.text: Correct — a mutant spec is the original spec seeded with one deliberate small change.

answer.text: A specification defect reported by users in the field

feedback.text: Mutant specs are artificial changes seeded on purpose, not field-reported defects.

answer.text: A test case derived from the specification

feedback.text: That is a test, not a mutant specification.

answer.text: An execution trace produced by a model checker

feedback.text: That is a counterexample/trace, not a mutant specification.

generalfeedback.text: A mutant specification is a variant of the specification produced by applying a spec mutation operator that makes one small change (e.g. negating a clause), just as a program mutant is a small change to code.

questiontext.text: In specification mutation, the artifact that is deliberately altered to create a mutant is:

answer.text: The specification / model

feedback.text: Correct — the spec or model is what gets mutated.

answer.text: The source code

feedback.text: Altering source code is program mutation, not specification mutation.

answer.text: The test harness

feedback.text: The test harness is infrastructure, not the mutated artifact.

answer.text: The input data files

feedback.text: Input data is not what a spec mutation operator changes.

generalfeedback.text: Specification mutation seeds a change into the specification or model (a requirement, an FSM, or a temporal property), leaving the program code untouched.

questiontext.text: The key difference between specification mutation and program (code) mutation is:

answer.text: Specification mutation changes the specification/model, whereas program mutation changes the program's source code

feedback.text: Correct — the two differ in which artifact is mutated.

answer.text: Specification mutation uses random inputs while program mutation is systematic

feedback.text: Both use systematic mutation operators; the difference is the artifact mutated.

answer.text: Specification mutation needs no mutation operators

feedback.text: Both rely on mutation operators; spec mutation just applies them to the spec.

answer.text: They are the same technique under two names

feedback.text: They are distinct: one mutates the spec, the other the code.

generalfeedback.text: Both are mutation techniques, but program mutation seeds faults into code and runs tests to detect them, while specification mutation seeds changes into the spec/model to assess or generate tests.

questiontext.text: A mutant specification is killed when:

answer.text: Some test or analysis distinguishes the behavior described by the mutant spec from that of the original spec

feedback.text: Correct — an observable difference between mutant and original spec kills it.

answer.text: The mutant specification fails to parse

feedback.text: A malformed mutant is discarded, not "killed" by distinguishing behavior.

answer.text: The mutant specification is longer than the original

feedback.text: Length is irrelevant to killing; killing requires a behavioral difference.

answer.text: The original specification is proven correct

feedback.text: Killing concerns distinguishing mutant from original, not proving correctness.

generalfeedback.text: A spec mutant is killed when a test case (or a model-checker run) reveals that the mutant specification and the original specification disagree on some behavior.

questiontext.text: An equivalent spec mutant is a mutant specification that:

answer.text: Is syntactically different from the original spec but semantically identical, so no test can distinguish them

feedback.text: Correct — identical meaning means it can never be killed.

answer.text: Is textually identical to the original specification

feedback.text: A mutation always introduces a syntactic change; identical text is not a mutant.

answer.text: Always contradicts the original specification

feedback.text: A contradicting mutant differs in meaning and is killable; an equivalent one has the same meaning.

answer.text: Cannot be expressed in the specification language

feedback.text: Equivalence is about meaning, not expressibility.

generalfeedback.text: An equivalent spec mutant differs syntactically from the original but denotes exactly the same behavior for every input, so no test or model-check can ever distinguish (kill) it.

questiontext.text: Model-based mutation testing refers to:

answer.text: Applying mutation operators to a behavioral model of the system (e.g. an FSM), rather than to the code

feedback.text: Correct — the model is mutated.

answer.text: Building a statistical model of how often each code mutant is killed

feedback.text: That is not what model-based mutation means; here the model is the mutated artifact.

answer.text: Mutating only the program's data model (database schema)

feedback.text: The "model" is a behavioral model/spec, not specifically a database schema.

answer.text: Randomly mutating the model checker's algorithm

feedback.text: The model checker is a tool, not the artifact being mutated.

generalfeedback.text: Model-based mutation testing seeds mutations into a model (such as an FSM or a formal specification) and uses the difference between the model and its mutants to assess or generate tests — a form of specification mutation.

questiontext.text: One purpose of specification mutation is to:

answer.text: Assess the adequacy of a test suite or the quality/completeness of the specification

feedback.text: Correct — killed mutants measure how well tests (or the spec) capture the intended behavior.

answer.text: Automatically repair defects in the program

feedback.text: Specification mutation evaluates or generates tests; it does not fix code.

answer.text: Prove the program has no defects

feedback.text: No mutation technique proves the absence of all defects.

answer.text: Compress the specification into fewer states

feedback.text: That is model minimization, not the purpose of specification mutation.

generalfeedback.text: Specification mutation is used to (a) assess the adequacy of a test suite or the quality of the specification and (b) generate tests. Measuring which spec mutants a suite kills gauges its adequacy.

questiontext.text: Specification mutation can be used to generate tests by:

answer.text: Using a model checker's counterexample from a mutated property as a test case

feedback.text: Correct — a counterexample that distinguishes the mutant from the original spec becomes a test.

answer.text: Compiling the mutant specification into an executable

feedback.text: Compiling a spec does not by itself produce test cases.

answer.text: Counting the number of clauses in the specification

feedback.text: Counting clauses is a metric, not a test-generation method.

answer.text: Removing all temporal operators from the specification

feedback.text: That would change the spec's meaning and does not generate tests.

generalfeedback.text: A model checker checking a mutated property against the model returns a counterexample — a trace where the mutant and original disagree. That trace is turned into a test case.

questiontext.text: Which is an example of a specification mutation operator?

answer.text: Negating a clause in a requirement (e.g. condition C becomes NOT C)

feedback.text: Correct — negating a requirement's clause mutates the specification.

answer.text: Deleting a line of C++ source in the implementation

feedback.text: That mutates code, so it is program mutation.

answer.text: Renaming a local variable in the program

feedback.text: That is a code-level change, not a specification change.

answer.text: Inserting a unary minus into a program expression

feedback.text: That is a code mutation operator (UOI), not a spec operator.

generalfeedback.text: Spec mutation operators change the specification: negate a clause, swap a relational/logical/temporal operator in a requirement, or redirect an FSM transition. Changes to source code are program mutation.

questiontext.text: In linear temporal logic, the operator G (globally) applied to a property p means that p:

answer.text: Holds in every state along the path (always)

feedback.text: Correct — G means "always / globally".

answer.text: Holds in at least one future state

feedback.text: That is F (eventually), not G.

answer.text: Holds only in the immediately next state

feedback.text: That is X (next), not G.

answer.text: Holds until some other property becomes true

feedback.text: That is the U (until) operator, not G.

generalfeedback.text: In LTL, G p ("globally p") asserts that p is true in every state of the execution path — the "always" operator.

questiontext.text: In linear temporal logic, F (eventually/finally) applied to p means that p:

answer.text: Holds in some current-or-future state

feedback.text: Correct — F means "eventually".

answer.text: Holds in every state along the path

feedback.text: That is G (globally), not F.

answer.text: Holds in the immediately next state only

feedback.text: That is X (next), not F.

answer.text: Never holds

feedback.text: F asserts p does hold at some point, the opposite of never.

generalfeedback.text: In LTL, F p ("eventually p") asserts that p becomes true at some state now or later along the path.

questiontext.text: When a model checker finds that a property is violated by the model, it produces a counterexample, which is:

answer.text: A concrete execution trace of the model that violates the property

feedback.text: Correct — the counterexample is a witnessing trace of the violation.

answer.text: A corrected version of the property that now holds

feedback.text: The checker returns a violating trace, not a rewritten property.

answer.text: A proof that the property holds on the model

feedback.text: A counterexample demonstrates a violation, not a proof of correctness.

answer.text: A random input unrelated to the model

feedback.text: A counterexample is a specific trace of the model, not a random input.

generalfeedback.text: A counterexample is a concrete sequence of states (an execution trace) of the model that demonstrates how the property is violated. This trace is exactly what specification-mutation test generation turns into a test.

questiontext.text: Which activity is specification mutation (not program mutation)?

answer.text: Replacing G with F in an LTL requirement and re-checking it against the model

feedback.text: Correct — the requirement (specification) was mutated.

answer.text: Replacing + with - in a C function and re-running the tests

feedback.text: That mutates code — program mutation.

answer.text: Deleting a statement in the source and re-running the tests

feedback.text: Deleting a source statement is program mutation.

answer.text: Inserting a unary minus in a program expression

feedback.text: That is a code-level (UOI) mutation.

generalfeedback.text: Changing a temporal-logic requirement (G to F) mutates the specification. Changing operators, statements, or expressions in the source code is program mutation.

questiontext.text: Specification mutation testing works by mutating the program's source code and running tests against it.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Mutating source code is program mutation. Specification mutation changes the specification/model instead.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Correct — specification mutation mutates the specification or model, not the source code (that would be program mutation).

generalfeedback.text: Specification mutation applies mutation operators to a specification or model (a requirement, an FSM, or a temporal property). Mutating source code is the separate technique of program mutation.

name.text: When a mutant spec is killed by a test

questiontext.text: A mutant specification is killed by a test case when:

answer.text: The test's expected result under the mutant spec differs from its expected result under the original spec

feedback.text: Correct — a test that the two specs would judge differently kills the mutant.

answer.text: The test executes quickly on the model checker

feedback.text: Execution speed has nothing to do with killing a mutant.

answer.text: The test passes on the original specification

feedback.text: Passing the original alone does not distinguish the mutant; disagreement between the two is required.

answer.text: The mutant specification has more states than the original

feedback.text: State count is irrelevant; killing requires a behavioral disagreement.

generalfeedback.text: A spec mutant is killed when some test would be judged differently by the mutant and by the original specification — i.e. the two specs disagree on that test's expected behavior.

questiontext.text: Applying a condition-negation spec mutation operator to the requirement guard temp > 100 yields which mutant?

answer.text: NOT (temp > 100)

feedback.text: Correct — condition negation wraps the guard in a logical NOT.

answer.text: temp >= 100

feedback.text: That is a relational-operator swap, not negation.

answer.text: temp > 200

feedback.text: That is an operand change, not negation.

answer.text: temp > 100 AND active

feedback.text: That adds a conjunct (guard strengthening), not negation.

generalfeedback.text: Condition negation replaces a requirement's condition C with NOT C. Here temp > 100 becomes NOT (temp > 100).

questiontext.text: Replacing >= with > in the requirement "the alarm sounds when pressure >= threshold" is a spec mutation operator that:

answer.text: Swaps a relational operator, changing the boundary behavior of the requirement

feedback.text: Correct — it alters what happens exactly at pressure = threshold.

answer.text: Deletes a clause from the requirement

feedback.text: No clause is removed; a relational operator is changed.

answer.text: Changes a temporal operator

feedback.text: No temporal operator is involved here.

answer.text: Redirects a state-machine transition

feedback.text: This is a relational change in a condition, not a transition redirection.

generalfeedback.text: Swapping a relational operator (here >= to >) changes the requirement's behavior at the boundary value pressure = threshold; a killing test must include that boundary.

questiontext.text: In an FSM specification, a mutation operator that changes a transition's destination (e.g. on input x the machine goes to state C instead of state B) is:

answer.text: Transition redirection — changing the target state of a transition

feedback.text: Correct — the transition's destination is altered.

answer.text: A relational-operator swap

feedback.text: No relational operator is involved; the transition target changed.

answer.text: A temporal-operator replacement

feedback.text: No temporal operator is involved.

answer.text: Condition negation

feedback.text: The guard is not negated; the destination state is changed.

generalfeedback.text: Redirecting a transition (changing where an input leads) is a standard FSM/model mutation operator. Other FSM operators change the triggering event or the guard.

questiontext.text: A spec mutation replaces AND with OR in a requirement's condition. Compared with the original, the mutated condition is:

answer.text: Weaker — it is satisfied in more cases (either operand true suffices)

feedback.text: Correct — AND needs both true; OR needs only one, so OR holds more often.

answer.text: Stronger — it is satisfied in fewer cases

feedback.text: OR is satisfied more often than AND, so it is weaker, not stronger.

answer.text: Unchanged in meaning

feedback.text: AND and OR differ whenever the operands have different truth values.

answer.text: Only affects arithmetic, not logic

feedback.text: AND/OR are logical connectives; the change is logical, not arithmetic.

generalfeedback.text: Replacing AND with OR (a logical-operator mutation, analogous to program mutation's LOR) weakens the condition: it now holds whenever either operand is true, a superset of the AND case.

name.text: Temporal operator mutation G to F

questiontext.text: A temporal-operator mutation replaces G p with F p in a property. This changes the requirement from:

answer.text: "p holds in every state" to "p holds in at least one state" — a strictly weaker requirement

feedback.text: Correct — G (always) becomes F (eventually), which is weaker.

answer.text: An equivalent restatement with the same meaning

feedback.text: G p and F p differ: G p implies F p, but not conversely.

answer.text: "p holds in some state" to "p holds in every state" — a stronger requirement

feedback.text: That is the reverse direction; G to F weakens the requirement.

answer.text: A change that only affects the next state

feedback.text: Next-state semantics belong to X, not to G or F.

generalfeedback.text: G p ("always p") requires p in every state; F p ("eventually p") requires p in some state. G p implies F p but not the reverse, so this mutation weakens the property and generally changes its meaning.

name.text: Counterexample as a test from a mutated property

questiontext.text: The original property p holds on model M. To generate a test from a mutant property p', you:

answer.text: Model-check p' against M; if M violates p', the counterexample trace is a test that distinguishes p' from p

feedback.text: Correct — the violating trace satisfies p (since M ⊨ p) but not p', so it distinguishes them.

answer.text: Model-check p against M again and discard the result

feedback.text: Re-checking the original property does not use the mutant and generates nothing new.

answer.text: Compile p' into code and profile it

feedback.text: Profiling a compiled property is not how tests are derived here.

answer.text: Count the states reachable in M

feedback.text: Counting states does not produce a distinguishing test.

generalfeedback.text: Model-checking the mutant property p' against M yields a counterexample when M violates p'. Because M satisfies the original p, that trace satisfies p but not p', so it distinguishes the two specifications and becomes a test.

name.text: Measuring test-suite adequacy with spec mutation

questiontext.text: To use specification mutation to measure a test suite's adequacy, you:

answer.text: Generate mutant specs and check what fraction of them the suite's tests distinguish from the original spec

feedback.text: Correct — the fraction of spec mutants killed measures adequacy.

answer.text: Count how many lines the specification has

feedback.text: Spec length is not an adequacy measure.

answer.text: Run the suite once against the original spec only

feedback.text: Without mutants there is nothing to kill, so no adequacy is measured.

answer.text: Remove every failing test from the suite

feedback.text: Removing tests does not measure adequacy against mutants.

generalfeedback.text: As with program mutation, you produce a set of spec mutants and see how many the test suite kills (distinguishes from the original). The proportion killed is an adequacy measure for the suite relative to the spec.

questiontext.text: During property-mutation test generation, a model checker reports that a mutated property still holds on the model (no counterexample). This means the mutant is:

answer.text: Equivalent with respect to that model — it cannot be killed via the model, so no test is produced

feedback.text: Correct — no counterexample means the model cannot distinguish mutant from original.

answer.text: Killed — the absence of a counterexample kills it

feedback.text: The opposite: a counterexample is what would distinguish (kill) it; its absence means it survives.

answer.text: Malformed and must be discarded

feedback.text: A well-formed mutant that still holds is equivalent, not malformed.

answer.text: Proof that the implementation is correct

feedback.text: It says nothing about the implementation, only about the model and this mutant.

generalfeedback.text: If the mutated property still holds on the model, there is no counterexample distinguishing it from the original with respect to that model — it is an equivalent mutant (relative to the model) and yields no test.

questiontext.text: Changing the triggering event on an FSM transition (e.g. it now fires on input "coin" instead of "button") is a spec mutation operator that:

answer.text: Alters which input causes the transition, potentially changing the accepted behavior

feedback.text: Correct — the transition now responds to a different input.

answer.text: Changes the number of states in the machine

feedback.text: The states are unchanged; only the triggering input changed.

answer.text: Negates a temporal-logic property

feedback.text: No temporal property is involved in an FSM event change.

answer.text: Deletes the transition entirely

feedback.text: The transition still exists; only its trigger changed.

generalfeedback.text: Mutating the event/input that fires a transition is a standard FSM mutation operator; it changes which inputs drive the machine and thus the specified behavior.

name.text: Why the counterexample makes a good test

questiontext.text: A counterexample obtained by model-checking a mutant property is a good test case because:

answer.text: It is a concrete trace where the mutant and original specifications disagree, so it can reveal whether an implementation follows the correct one

feedback.text: Correct — it targets exactly the behavior that distinguishes the two specs.

answer.text: It is chosen at random, giving broad coverage

feedback.text: A counterexample is targeted, not random.

answer.text: It always exercises every state of the model

feedback.text: A counterexample is a single trace, not a tour of all states.

answer.text: It proves the specification is complete

feedback.text: A counterexample distinguishes two specs; it does not prove completeness.

generalfeedback.text: The counterexample is a concrete execution where the original and mutant specs diverge. Running it against an implementation checks whether the implementation obeys the intended (original) spec rather than the mutated (faulty) one.

questiontext.text: You have an SMV model and an LTL requirement. You alter the LTL formula and re-run the model checker. This is:

answer.text: Specification (property) mutation, since the requirement — not the code — was changed

feedback.text: Correct — the LTL requirement is part of the specification.

answer.text: Program mutation, since the model checker ran the model

feedback.text: Running the checker does not make it program mutation; the mutated artifact was the requirement.

answer.text: Fuzz testing, since inputs were varied

feedback.text: No random inputs were fuzzed; a formula was mutated.

answer.text: Neither — changing a formula is not a mutation

feedback.text: Changing the LTL formula is exactly a specification mutation.

generalfeedback.text: Mutating an LTL/CTL requirement and re-checking it is specification mutation: the mutated artifact is the requirement (part of the spec), not the program code.

questiontext.text: A spec mutation replaces one operand with another in a requirement, turning level > max into level > min. This is:

answer.text: An operand (variable) replacement mutation on the specification

feedback.text: Correct — a variable operand was swapped for another.

answer.text: A relational-operator swap

feedback.text: The relational operator > is unchanged; an operand was replaced.

answer.text: A temporal-operator replacement

feedback.text: No temporal operator is involved.

answer.text: A transition redirection

feedback.text: No FSM transition is involved; this is a condition-operand change.

generalfeedback.text: Replacing a variable operand (here max with min) is an operand/variable-replacement spec mutation, analogous to variable replacement in program mutation.

questiontext.text: Instead of mutating a property, model-based mutation testing can mutate the model itself and then:

answer.text: Check the original requirements against the mutant model; a requirement now violated yields a counterexample distinguishing the two models

feedback.text: Correct — the counterexample separates the original model from the mutant.

answer.text: Delete all requirements and keep only the mutant model

feedback.text: Requirements are needed to detect the mutant's difference; you do not delete them.

answer.text: Mutate the source code as well to match

feedback.text: Model mutation changes the model, not the code.

answer.text: Run the mutant model without any properties

feedback.text: Without properties there is nothing for the checker to violate, so no test emerges.

generalfeedback.text: One can mutate the model and check the original requirements against it. If the mutant model violates a requirement the original satisfied, the counterexample is a trace distinguishing model from mutant — a test that kills the model mutant.

questiontext.text: Mutating x >= 5 to x > 5 in a requirement changes the specified behavior:

answer.text: Only at x = 5; a killing test must include that boundary value

feedback.text: Correct — the two conditions agree everywhere except x = 5.

answer.text: For all values of x

feedback.text: They agree for every x except exactly 5.

answer.text: Only for negative x

feedback.text: They agree for negative x; they differ only at x = 5.

answer.text: Never — the mutant is equivalent

feedback.text: It is not equivalent: x = 5 distinguishes >= from >.

generalfeedback.text: x >= 5 and x > 5 differ only at x = 5 (true vs false). A test that omits the boundary would fail to kill this mutant, so the killing test must include x = 5.

questiontext.text: A requirement's guard NOT (a AND b) is mutated to NOT a OR NOT b. This mutant is:

answer.text: Equivalent — by De Morgan's law the two forms are logically identical, so no test can kill it

feedback.text: Correct — NOT (a AND b) is exactly NOT a OR NOT b.

answer.text: Killed by any test where a and b differ

feedback.text: The two forms agree on every assignment, so no test distinguishes them.

answer.text: Non-equivalent because OR replaced AND

feedback.text: The surrounding negations make the whole expression equivalent under De Morgan's law.

answer.text: Malformed and therefore discarded

feedback.text: It is well-formed and logically equivalent, not malformed.

generalfeedback.text: De Morgan's law states NOT (a AND b) is equivalent to NOT a OR NOT b. The mutant denotes the identical boolean function, so it is an equivalent spec mutant that no test can kill.

name.text: Is G to F an equivalent mutation?

questiontext.text: Is replacing G p by F p in a property an equivalent mutation?

answer.text: No — G p (always) and F p (eventually) have different meanings (G p implies F p but not conversely), so it generally changes the spec and is killable

feedback.text: Correct — the two operators are not interchangeable.

answer.text: Yes — G and F always mean the same thing

feedback.text: They do not: "always" is strictly stronger than "eventually".

answer.text: Yes — F p implies G p, so they coincide

feedback.text: F p does not imply G p; the implication runs the other way.

answer.text: No — but only because F is undefined in LTL

feedback.text: F is a standard LTL operator; the reason is the difference in meaning, not undefinedness.

generalfeedback.text: G p requires p in every state; F p only requires p somewhere. G p implies F p, but not the reverse, so the mutation changes the property's meaning — it is non-equivalent and generally killable (a trace where p holds sometime but not always distinguishes them).

name.text: Why a mutant property yields a distinguishing counterexample

questiontext.text: Model-checking a mutant property p' against a model M (with the original p true on M) yields a counterexample. Why does that trace distinguish the mutant from the original?

answer.text: The trace is an execution of M that violates p'; since M satisfies p, the same trace satisfies p, so p and p' disagree on it

feedback.text: Correct — the trace satisfies p but not p', exactly distinguishing them.

answer.text: The counterexample is generated independently of both p and p'

feedback.text: The counterexample is specifically a violation of p', so it is tied to the mutant.

answer.text: Because p' is syntactically longer than p

feedback.text: Syntactic length is irrelevant; the distinguishing power comes from the semantic disagreement on the trace.

answer.text: Because the model checker rewrites p to match p'

feedback.text: The checker does not rewrite the original; it finds a trace violating p'.

generalfeedback.text: The counterexample violates p' by construction. Because M satisfies the original p, every trace of M (including this one) satisfies p. So the trace satisfies p but not p' — a concrete witness that the two specifications differ, which is why it works as a test.

questiontext.text: A clause of a requirement is mutated, but no test (and no model-check) can ever kill the resulting mutant. This most likely indicates:

answer.text: The mutant is equivalent, which suggests the clause is redundant or the spec is over-constrained — it does not affect the specified behavior

feedback.text: Correct — an unkillable mutation points to a clause with no effect on meaning.

answer.text: The test suite is perfectly adequate

feedback.text: An unkillable mutant is equivalent; it says nothing positive about suite adequacy.

answer.text: The specification is guaranteed complete

feedback.text: Equivalence of one mutant does not imply completeness of the whole spec.

answer.text: The program contains a fault

feedback.text: This is about the spec's structure, not a program fault.

generalfeedback.text: If mutating a clause never changes the specified behavior, the mutant is equivalent — evidence that the clause is redundant or the requirement over-constrained. Specification mutation can thus expose redundancy and help assess spec quality.

questiontext.text: A team seeds a fault into a CTL property, re-runs the model checker to obtain a counterexample, and turns it into a test. Which best describes this?

answer.text: Specification (model-based) mutation testing — the property was mutated, and the counterexample becomes a test

feedback.text: Correct — mutating a CTL property and deriving a test from the counterexample is specification mutation.

answer.text: Program mutation — because a test was produced at the end

feedback.text: Producing a test does not make it program mutation; the mutated artifact was the property.

answer.text: Structural code coverage measurement

feedback.text: No code structure was measured; a property was mutated.

answer.text: Equivalence-class partitioning of the input domain

feedback.text: That is a black-box input-partition technique, unrelated to mutating a CTL property.

generalfeedback.text: Seeding a fault into a temporal (CTL) property and using the model checker's counterexample as a test is specification/model-based mutation: the mutated artifact is the property, and the counterexample distinguishes it from the original.

questiontext.text: A property F p is mutated to F F p ("eventually eventually p"). This mutant is:

answer.text: Equivalent — F is idempotent, so F F p is logically the same as F p and cannot be killed

feedback.text: Correct — F F p ≡ F p.

answer.text: Non-equivalent — F F p requires p twice

feedback.text: F F p does not require p "twice"; it reduces to F p.

answer.text: Non-equivalent — it is stronger than F p

feedback.text: They are equal in strength; F F p ≡ F p.

answer.text: Malformed — F cannot be nested

feedback.text: Nesting temporal operators is allowed; here it simply collapses to F p.

generalfeedback.text: The eventually operator is idempotent: F F p is equivalent to F p (likewise G G p ≡ G p). So this mutation produces an equivalent spec mutant that no test can kill.

questiontext.text: Two major practical limitations of specification/model mutation testing are:

answer.text: Detecting equivalent mutants is hard (undecidable in general), and model-checking many mutants can suffer state-space explosion

feedback.text: Correct — equivalent mutants and model size are the classic limitations.

answer.text: Mutation operators cannot be defined for specifications, and models never have states

feedback.text: Spec mutation operators are well defined, and models do have states.

answer.text: Model checkers cannot produce counterexamples, and specs cannot be mutated

feedback.text: Both are false: checkers produce counterexamples and specs can be mutated.

answer.text: It requires source code and cannot use a model

feedback.text: The opposite — it works on a spec/model and needs no source code.

generalfeedback.text: Like program mutation, specification mutation faces the equivalent-mutant problem (equivalence is undecidable in general). Additionally, checking many mutant properties/models against a large model can hit state-space explosion, limiting scalability.

name.text: No counterexample means equivalent w.r.t. model

questiontext.text: In property-mutation test generation, a mutant property that the model still satisfies:

answer.text: Yields no counterexample and hence no test — it is an equivalent mutant relative to the model

feedback.text: Correct — with nothing to violate, the model cannot distinguish it from the original.

answer.text: Yields the strongest possible test

feedback.text: No counterexample means no test at all is produced.

answer.text: Proves the original property was wrong

feedback.text: It says nothing about the original property being wrong.

answer.text: Forces the model checker to enumerate all traces as tests

feedback.text: No violation means no counterexample; the checker does not emit all traces.

generalfeedback.text: If the model satisfies the mutant property, the model checker returns no counterexample, so no distinguishing test can be generated — the mutant is equivalent with respect to that model.

questiontext.text: In an FSM spec, a mutation strengthens a transition guard by adding an extra conjunct (guard becomes g AND extra). Relative to the original, the mutated transition:

answer.text: Fires in fewer cases (a subset of the original); a killing test must reach an input where the original fired but the mutant does not

feedback.text: Correct — adding a conjunct can only shrink the set of firing inputs.

answer.text: Fires in more cases than before

feedback.text: Adding a conjunct makes the guard harder to satisfy, so it fires less often.

answer.text: Fires in exactly the same cases

feedback.text: Only if the extra conjunct were always true given g; in general the guard is strictly narrower.

answer.text: Never fires under any input

feedback.text: It still fires whenever both g and the extra conjunct hold.

generalfeedback.text: Strengthening a guard with an added conjunct restricts firing to a subset of the original cases. A test that kills this mutant must reach an input where the original guard held but the strengthened guard does not.

questiontext.text: A requirement condition a OR b is mutated to NOT (NOT a AND NOT b). This mutant is:

answer.text: Equivalent — by De Morgan's law it denotes the same function as a OR b, so it cannot be killed

feedback.text: Correct — NOT (NOT a AND NOT b) is exactly a OR b.

answer.text: Non-equivalent because AND now appears

feedback.text: The negations restore the OR meaning under De Morgan's law.

answer.text: Killed whenever exactly one of a, b is true

feedback.text: Both forms give true then, so they still agree; no test distinguishes them.

answer.text: Only equivalent when a equals b

feedback.text: They agree on all four assignments, not only when a equals b.

generalfeedback.text: De Morgan's law gives a OR b is equivalent to NOT (NOT a AND NOT b). The mutant computes the identical boolean function, so it is an equivalent spec mutant.

questiontext.text: A requirement a AND (a OR b) is mutated to a AND (a OR c) (operand b replaced by c). The mutant is:

answer.text: Equivalent — by absorption a AND (a OR anything) reduces to a, so both forms equal a; this also reveals the second clause is redundant

feedback.text: Correct — the value depends only on a, so replacing b by c changes nothing.

answer.text: Killed by any test where b and c differ

feedback.text: Since the whole expression equals a, the value of b or c never matters; no such test kills it.

answer.text: Non-equivalent because c is a new variable

feedback.text: Introducing c has no effect: the expression reduces to a regardless.

answer.text: Stronger than the original

feedback.text: Both are equivalent to a; neither is stronger.

generalfeedback.text: By the absorption law, a AND (a OR X) equals a for any X. So both the original and the mutant equal a, making the mutant equivalent. Its unkillability exposes that the "(a OR ...)" clause is redundant in the requirement.

name.text: Trap property to witness a behavior

questiontext.text: A model checker returns a trace only when a property is violated. To obtain a trace that witnesses a desired behavior B (for use as a test), you can:

answer.text: Assert a "trap" property claiming B never occurs; the model checker's counterexample is then a trace exhibiting B

feedback.text: Correct — negating the behavior of interest makes the counterexample a witness of it.

answer.text: Assert that B always occurs and take the proof as the test

feedback.text: A proof (no violation) yields no trace; you need a violated property to get a counterexample.

answer.text: Disable the model checker and enumerate inputs by hand

feedback.text: The trap-property technique uses the checker itself; manual enumeration is not the method.

answer.text: Remove all properties so every trace is a counterexample

feedback.text: With no property there is nothing to violate, so no counterexample is produced.

generalfeedback.text: Because a counterexample is produced only for a violated property, test-generation methods assert a "trap" (never-claim) property stating the behavior of interest never happens. The model checker then returns a counterexample that is exactly a trace realizing that behavior.

questiontext.text: A property p is mutated to X p (next p). In general this mutant is:

answer.text: Non-equivalent — X p refers to the next state, so it differs from p evaluated at the current state

feedback.text: Correct — shifting the evaluation point by one state generally changes meaning.

answer.text: Equivalent — X p always means the same as p

feedback.text: X p is about the next state, not the current one, so it differs in general.

answer.text: Equivalent — because every path repeats

feedback.text: Paths do not generally repeat, and even so X shifts the evaluation point.

answer.text: Malformed — X cannot be applied to an atomic property

feedback.text: X can be applied to any subformula, including an atomic one.

generalfeedback.text: X p asserts p holds in the next state, whereas p asserts it in the current state. On a path where p holds now but not next (or vice versa), the two differ, so the mutation is generally non-equivalent and killable.

questiontext.text: A logical-operand-swap mutation changes a side-effect-free spec condition a AND b to b AND a. This mutant is:

answer.text: Equivalent — AND is commutative in a side-effect-free specification, so the two forms are identical and cannot be killed

feedback.text: Correct — order of operands does not matter for a pure boolean condition.

answer.text: Non-equivalent because the operands were reordered

feedback.text: Reordering a commutative operator does not change a side-effect-free condition's meaning.

answer.text: Killed by any test where a and b differ

feedback.text: a AND b and b AND a agree on every assignment, so no such test kills it.

answer.text: Equivalent only when a equals b

feedback.text: They agree on all assignments, not only when a equals b.

generalfeedback.text: Boolean AND is commutative, so in a specification without evaluation-order side effects, a AND b equals b AND a. The mutant denotes the same function — an equivalent spec mutant. (In short-circuiting code with side effects, order can matter; that is a program, not spec, concern.)

name.text: Value of a test from a killed spec mutant

questiontext.text: A test derived from a killed spec mutant is valuable because, when executed on an implementation, it:

answer.text: Distinguishes the original spec's behavior from the mutant's, so an implementation that matches the mutated (faulty) spec instead of the original will fail

feedback.text: Correct — the test targets exactly the behavior on which the two specs disagree.

answer.text: Guarantees the implementation is free of all faults

feedback.text: One targeted test cannot prove global correctness.

answer.text: Exercises every path in the implementation

feedback.text: It is a single distinguishing trace, not a full path tour.

answer.text: Is independent of both the original and mutant specs

feedback.text: It is derived precisely from where the two specs differ, so it depends on both.

generalfeedback.text: The killing test is a trace where the original and mutant specs disagree. Running it against an implementation checks whether the implementation follows the intended (original) behavior; an implementation exhibiting the mutant's faulty behavior would fail the test.
